I have farmed these 10.1 mu in Quzhou for 40 years. I finished high school, so I read the nutrient numbers on fertilizer bags myself and I figure the cost per jin before I buy anything. My husband and I are two people. He works off-farm in a factory in Handan for half the year, which brings in cash, but it means I handle most of the spraying and watering alone. We have our own well, so I can irrigate when I need to, but every time I start the pump the electricity bill adds up. I count every yuan.

My land is all wheat-maize rotation, same as every household in our village. Last year my wheat made about 500 kg per mu — not bad, but the maize only made about 580 kg per mu because August turned dry and I was two days late with the grain-filling water. I will not let that happen again.

For wheat this year: I will plant Jimai 32, an improved variety. My neighbor Li switched to it last year and got 550 kg per mu on his field next to mine, so I will follow. I need 30 jin of seed per mu, which is 303 jin total for the 10.1 mu. After the maize comes off in early October, I will rotary till to break up the stalk residue and prepare a level seedbed. For fertilizer, I put down 50 kg per mu of compound fertilizer — I buy the 18-22-5 type, which comes in 50-kg bags at 11 yuan per bag. That is about 11 bags for 121 yuan. From this base I get 9 kg of nitrogen, 11 kg of phosphorus, and 2.5 kg of potassium per mu. Then at the wheat jointing stage in late March, when the stems are starting to elongate, I top-dress with 20 kg per mu of urea. The urea is 46% nitrogen, so that adds another 9.2 kg of nitrogen per mu. I also spread 5 kg per mu of potassium chloride because the soil tests I did with the county extension three years ago showed potassium is on the low side here, and I noticed last year's stalks were a bit thin. Total nutrient input comes to about 18 kg nitrogen, 11 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I irrigate three times: the winter water in early December to protect the seedlings from freezing, the jointing water in late March, and the grain-filling water in mid-May. For pesticides, I spray four times: herbicide once when the wheat is greening up in spring, insecticide once at heading for aphids, and fungicide twice — once for powdery mildew and once for rust. I expect 520 kg per mu if the spring rain cooperates.

For maize: I plant Denghai 605, a hybrid seed that costs 60 yuan per 1.2-kg bag, and I need 1.2 kg per mu — 12 bags total, 720 yuan. Right after the wheat harvest in early June there is no time to plow; I hire my neighbor's no-till planter for 20 yuan per mu and seed directly into the wheat stubble. At planting I apply 50 kg per mu of compound fertilizer, the 26-8-8 type. That gives me 13 kg nitrogen, 4 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium per mu from the base. Then at the big trumpet stage in late July, when the plants are shoulder-high and the tassels are forming, I side-dress with 6 kg per mu of urea, which adds another 2.8 kg of nitrogen. Total nitrogen is about 16 kg per mu. I also add a small amount of phosphorus and potassium fertilizer to bring both up to 5 kg per mu — the maize needs a balanced diet to set big ears. I irrigate twice: the critical water at the trumpet stage in late July, and the grain-filling water in mid-August. Two good waterings are enough if you time them right. For pesticides, I spray three times: herbicide once after emergence to control crabgrass, and insecticide twice — once for corn borer at the trumpet stage and once for armyworm in August. I expect 600 kg per mu this year.

I know the fertilizer bills are high. The wheat inputs run about 1,400 yuan and the maize inputs about 1,600 yuan for the 10.1 mu. But I have done the math: if I cut 50 kg of urea to save 80 yuan, and the yield drops by 30 kg per mu, I lose 300 yuan at current grain prices. A bad harvest is a disaster; wasting a little fertilizer is just a cost. I would rather apply a bit too much than risk coming up short.
